title: Chesed and Gevurah
hookLine: Chesed and Gevurah: giving freely, and holding back
carry: chesed gives freely; gevurah gives it shape
tomorrow: Tiferet, the heart of the tree

cards: A river with no banks isn't a river. It's a flood. It goes everywhere, soaks everything, and reaches nothing in particular.
A river that's all banks and no water is just a ditch. What makes a river is both: the water that wants to pour out, and the edges that give it a direction. Parents know this one.
So do good friends, and good teachers. Give with no limit and the gift drowns the person. Hold back with no love and the limit turns cruel.

teach.h: TWO ARMS: ONE REACHES, ONE HOLDS.
teach.b: Chesed. Love, kindness, giving freely. And its partner, Gevurah: strength, restraint, holding back.
First, where they sit. On the kabbalists' map, Chesed is on the right and Gevurah on the left, like two arms. One reaches out.
One holds firm. Second, their faces.
Chesed is linked to Abraham, whose tent in Genesis is open, who runs to feed three strangers in the heat of the day.
The prophet Micah closes his book saying God will perform "the mercy to Abraham", and in Hebrew that mercy is chesed. Gevurah is linked to Isaac, the son who was bound on the altar and lived.
Jacob even calls God "the fear of Isaac". Kindness and awe, two fathers, two sides. Third, the images.
Kabbalists pair Chesed with water, which flows to whatever is lowest, and Gevurah with fire, which burns away and draws lines. Water alone floods. Fire alone scorches.
Fourth, the surprise. Gevurah isn't the villain.

teach.h: LIMITS ARE A KIND OF CARE.
teach.b: Limits are a kind of care. A parent who says not tonight, a friend who says I won't help you do that, a teacher who returns your work marked up: that's Gevurah, and it can be loving.
Some teachers say even the making of the world needed both: love to give, and limits to give it shape. Neither side is meant to win. Too much of either, kabbalists say, and the world tips over.

how: Jewish teachers often speak of acts of chesed, loving-kindness, such as visiting the sick and feeding guests; in Kabbalah and Hasidic thought, Chesed and Gevurah are taught as a pair of qualities a person learns to balance.

o: awe and holding back before God
strict justice that punishes every wrong

games.q: love and limits — tap the pairs.

s: in Kabbalah, Gevurah is the villain of the map
limits are a kind of care. neither side is meant to win.
Micah's "mercy to Abraham" is chesed in Hebrew
the prophet closes his book with it.
Chesed with water, which flows; Gevurah with fire, which draws lines.

games.q: a friend asks you, again, to cover for them in a way that's hurting them. in this picture, what's the loving move?
o: hold a limit, with love behind it.
games.why: Chesed alone floods; Gevurah alone scorches. kabbalists say the world needs both, held together.

practice: Let your right hand rest open on your knee and think of one place where you give, maybe until it floods; then let your left hand close gently and think of one place where you hold back, maybe until it burns.
Rest both hands still, and ask, without judging yourself, which one needs a little more of the other.

wordCard.voice: Chesed. Love and kindness, giving freely: the right arm of the sefirot, linked to Abraham and to water, held in balance by Gevurah, strength and restraint. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: loving-kindness, mercy. The sefirah on the right side of the map.

carryVoice: Your line: chesed gives freely; gevurah gives it shape. A river needs both water and banks. Tomorrow, the light in the middle.
